newsitem.title: USA: Communications re-established with Mars rover.
newsitem.headline: Communications re-established with Mars rover.

text.p: Relieved space scientists re-established communications with the Mars Pathfinder rover on Monday after a weekend during which the little buggy and its landing craft refused to phone home.
"So far the scientists don't have an explanation for what happened, they're still looking into it," Jet Propulsion Laboratory spokesman Alan Wood said of the breakdown in communications.
He said scientists re-established contact with the landing craft at 2:45 a.m. PDT (0945 GMT) on Monday after losing the signal on Saturday night.
The spacecraft, on command from Earth, started sending a stream of engineering data telling scientists the lander and rover were in fine shape, Wood said.
The communications session, using both the lander's antennas, lasted about 6 1/2 hours, Wood said. He did not know if any scientific data had been relayed from Mars to Earth during that time.
Scientists expected to know more about the problem by the time they hold a scheduled news conference on Tuesday.

For the second weekend in a row Pathfinder took an unexpected two-day break. Communications were lost the previous weekend in a series of computer glitches that project scientist Matthew Golombek said "impacted us severely," putting Sojourner several days behind in its rock sampling tasks.

Computer scientist Glen Reeves explained last week that the computer on board the Pathfinder landing craft had reset itself three times when it sensed an overload, automatically cutting communications with Earth.

This was the result of a built-in safety measure in the software programme. "An analogy would be when your PC (personal computer) locks up and you reach around the back and hit the reset button," Reeves said.
It was not known if the same problems caused this weekend's blackout.

It was also not known what impact the setback would have on the mission, but Golombek stressed last week that the six-wheeled rover, which is about the size of a microwave oven, could operate on the Martian surface "indefinitely" and its mission had already been extended to a long-term project, meaning it would return more data to Earth than had originally been planned. Pathfinder landed on Mars on July 4.

The rover, using its alpha protein X-ray spectrometer, has already analysed two Martian rocks, dubbed Yogi and Barnacle Bill, and found them to be different in composition although still somewhat resembling rocks on Earth.
Scientists speculated that both or one of the rocks might have been swept into the landing site area in the Ares Vallis basin by a devastating flood they believe occurred about 4.5 billion years ago.

Scientists also wanted the rover to take a stroll through a clump of rocks they have named The Cabbage Patch and take an analysis of a white rock -- the only one of its kind near the landing site -- dubbed Scooby Doo.
Other targets for the rover included rocks named Half Dome, Witch, Shark and Flat Top.

The JPL team was also working on what it promises will be the most exciting panorama of Mars yet produced by the mission -- a composite of thousands of postage stamp-sized frames put together to produce a 12-colour "Gallery Pan" of the Martian surface, covering 360 degrees and showing expansive views from the lander to the horizon.
